content: The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that all individuals diagnosed with HIV should be offered voluntary provider-assisted referral services. This approach aims to facilitate HIV testing services (HTS) for their sexual and drug-injecting partners. Some individuals with HIV may prefer that healthcare providers disclose their HIV status to their partners, while others may choose not to disclose this information. Providers must engage in discussions with their clients to explore the most suitable and preferred disclosure method based on the specific dynamics of the client’s relationships. For further details on service delivery options, refer to Chapter 5. Individuals who decline provider-assisted referral services and prefer to disclose their HIV status directly to their partners should be encouraged and supported in doing so. Disclosure methods may vary depending on the partner. For instance, an individual may choose to personally disclose their status to a primary partner but opt for provider-assisted referral for other partners. Providers are responsible for determining, in collaboration with the client, the most appropriate disclosure method for each partner. It is important to note that distributing a self-test kit to a partner or encouraging them to access HTS does not necessarily require the individual to disclose their HIV status or self-test results. Individuals with reactive self-test results should be informed that a reactive result is not equivalent to a confirmed HIV-positive diagnosis. Partners who self-test together and receive reactive results require further confirmatory testing to establish their HIV status. Healthcare workers involved in the care of an HIV-positive client must be informed of the diagnosis as necessary to ensure appropriate follow-up care. However, this disclosure must respect the client’s right to privacy and confidentiality. Some clients may need time to process their diagnosis before they are ready to disclose their status to their partners, which may occur during subsequent visits. Trained providers distributing HIV self-testing (HIVST) kits may inquire about test results as part of follow-up care, but self-testers should be informed that sharing their results is entirely voluntary. Disclosure of HIV test results to law enforcement or legal authorities is considered unethical unless the client has provided explicit written consent. Linkage to care and treatment is a critical component of HTS. Without linkage to care, the value of HIV testing and learning one’s status is limited. Individuals who test HIV-negative but remain at ongoing risk should be linked to prevention services. Those with reactive self-test results must be connected to further confirmatory testing and additional services as needed. HTS sites, testers, and counselors are responsible for ensuring linkage to care by providing post-test service packages, which include evidence-based counseling messages and support tools tailored to the context, setting, and population. Linkage to antiretroviral therapy (ART) is essential for all individuals diagnosed with HIV. WHO recommends initiating ART as early as possible following diagnosis. Individuals who were previously diagnosed with HIV but are not currently on ART should be supported to re-engage in care and initiate or reinitiate treatment. This group may include individuals diagnosed before the “treat all” era, those who were not ready to start ART when it was first offered, and those who discontinued treatment. Retesting may be necessary to facilitate re-linkage to care and treatment. For individuals testing HIV-negative but at ongoing risk, linkage to specific prevention interventions, such as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), may be beneficial. Programs should monitor linkage to care within 30 to 90 days of an HIV-positive diagnosis and track ART initiation within 7 to 14 days. Linkage to prevention services following HTS is less commonly monitored but may be reported as part of prevention program data. Rapid ART initiation should be offered to all individuals with a confirmed HIV diagnosis following clinical assessment. This approach is particularly important for individuals with advanced HIV disease or very low CD4 cell counts, as they are at higher risk of mortality. Same-day ART initiation should be prioritized where feasible, and clients should be fully informed of the benefits of ART. However, individuals should not be coerced into starting treatment immediately and should be supported in making an informed decision about when to begin ART. Integrated and co-located services, where HTS and ART are readily available, facilitate linkage to care. In settings where co-location is not feasible, peer support, navigation services, and case management can help ensure effective linkage to prevention, treatment, and care. Accelerating ART initiation through same-day diagnosis and treatment is particularly beneficial for individuals presenting with advanced HIV disease. WHO recommends discontinuing the use of Western blotting in HIV testing strategies and prioritizing simpler rapid diagnostic tests that provide same-day results. Differentiated ART delivery models, peer support, and adherence counseling are necessary to improve retention in care and prevent treatment drop-out, especially for key populations, men, young people, and pregnant women. Community-based HTS and HIVST have demonstrated comparable linkage rates to conventional facility-based services, particularly for individuals who might not otherwise test or access care.
